boundary: which allocator owns the object the defect touches: pymalloc (nested) or libc malloc (non-nested). Decided per case by MEASUREMENT, not by the object's size -- the ASan heap report is run twice and the question is whether it SURVIVES PYTHONMALLOC=pymalloc
title: CPython 3.13.7 spatial defects at the pymalloc boundary, plus temporal and spatial defects whose memory comes straight from libc malloc
note: A sibling of pymalloc-repros, not an addition to it. That corpus is scoped to consumer-side TEMPORAL defects whose memory comes from pymalloc and asserts completeness -- 20 cases, expect_live_in_pin {true: 20}, and a shape_prose regex matching "[Tt]wenty reports" in its README -- so adding a spatial or a libc-malloc case there would falsify the claim and break its own prose check. Its 20 cover the temporal/nested cell; these 21 are the four cells: 13 spatial/nested, 5 spatial/non-nested, 3 temporal/non-nested. Liveness and the nested/non-nested side are both measured on the pinned ASan build and nothing here is inferred from a commit message or a CPE. The arms are named as pymalloc-repros names them, so the two corpora read side by side: spatial is base Capstone, sublet is the same heap plus patch 0014. All three arms have been run; results/20261006/ carries the matrix, so every arm is declared "not written" and status is built rather than measured. Cases 03 and 04 are two triggers for one fix (gh-140492), so the 32 cases cover 31 distinct upstream fixes. Cases 22-32 are the same upstream issues pymalloc-repros holds as C models, so this corpus is not disjoint from it: the scope is the four cells, and those eleven are here because a C model and an interpreter run of one defect are not the same measurement -- on the base arm the C models all complete while three of the eleven fault, all with cause 24. Each of the eleven carries a sibling_issue pointer to its C model.
